pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Discuss the blood circulatory system in humans and the composition and functions of blood.
- Explain the functions of the parts of the circulatory system.
- Draw and label the longitudinal section of a mammalian heart.

pages.title: What is the Circulatory System?
pages.body: The circulatory system is the network of the heart, blood and blood vessels that works together to transport blood, and the substances it carries, to every part of the body. Without a functioning circulatory system, oxygen, nutrients, hormones and other essential substances would have no way of reaching the billions of cells that make up the human body, and waste products would have no way of being carried away for disposal.

questions.q: The circulatory system mainly consists of
o: The heart, blood and blood vessels
questions.e: The circulatory system is the network of the heart, blood and blood vessels that works together to transport blood, and the substances it carries, to every part of the body.

pages.title: The Composition of Blood
pages.body: Plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets are the four main components of blood, each contributing a distinct role. Plasma is the pale yellow, liquid part of blood, made mostly of water, that carries dissolved nutrients, hormones, waste products and blood cells around the body. Red blood cells, described in an earlier grade, are the most numerous blood cells and carry oxygen throughout the body using the protein haemoglobin. White blood cells defend the body against infection by identifying and destroying harmful microorganisms. Platelets are small cell fragments that help blood clot at the site of an injury, sealing wounds and preventing excessive blood loss.

pages.title: Functions of Blood
pages.body: Transporting substances, defending against disease, and regulating body conditions are the three broad functions blood performs for the body. Blood transports oxygen from the lungs, nutrients from the digestive system, hormones from glands, and waste products such as carbon (IV) oxide and urea to the organs responsible for removing them. Blood defends the body through the activity of white blood cells and clotting factors, protecting against infection and blood loss. Blood also helps regulate body temperature, by carrying heat around the body, and helps maintain a stable internal environment more generally, a state called homeostasis.

questions.e: Plasma is the pale yellow, liquid part of blood, made mostly of water, that carries dissolved nutrients, hormones, waste products and blood cells around the body.

questions.q: Which blood component helps the body fight infection?
questions.e: White blood cells defend the body against infection by identifying and destroying harmful microorganisms.

questions.q: Which blood component helps blood clot at a wound?
questions.e: Platelets are small cell fragments that help blood clot at the site of an injury, sealing wounds and preventing excessive blood loss.

lessons.title: Parts of the Circulatory System and Their Functions

pages.title: Parts of the Circulatory System and Their Functions
pages.body: The heart, arteries, veins and capillaries are the four main parts of the circulatory system, and this lesson treats each one individually to explain its specific structure and function.

pages.title: The Heart
pages.body:
The heart is a muscular, fist sized organ located slightly to the left of the centre of the chest, divided internally into four chambers, two upper chambers called atria and two lower chambers called ventricles. The heart's main function is to act as a pump, contracting rhythmically to push blood out into the arteries and around the body, then relaxing to allow blood returning through the veins to refill its chambers before the next contraction. One way valves within the heart ensure blood flows in a single direction through the chambers, preventing backflow.

[[pic:A labelled longitudinal section diagram of a mammalian heart, clearly showing the four chambers (right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle), the major blood vessels entering and leaving the heart (vena cava, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein, aorta), and the heart valves, with arrows indicating the direction of blood flow through the heart.]]

Notice how blood entering the right side of the heart is deoxygenated, having returned from the body, while blood entering the left side of the heart is oxygenated, having returned from the lungs, and how the heart's internal structure keeps these two blood supplies properly separated as they pass through.

questions.q: The heart has how many chambers?
questions.e: The Heart The heart is a muscular, fist sized organ located slightly to the left of the centre of the chest, divided internally into four chambers, two upper chambers called atria and two lower chambers called ventricles.

questions.q: The upper chambers of the heart are called
questions.e: The Heart The heart is a muscular, fist sized organ located slightly to the left of the centre of the chest, divided internally into four chambers, two upper chambers called atria and two lower chambers called ventricles.

pages.title: Arteries
pages.body: Arteries are thick walled, muscular blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart, usually under high pressure, since they must withstand the force of each heartbeat. With the important exception of the pulmonary artery, which carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs, most arteries carry oxygenated blood to the tissues of the body. Their thick, elastic walls allow arteries to expand slightly with each heartbeat and then recoil, helping to maintain a steady flow of blood between beats.

pages.title: Veins
pages.body: Veins are thinner walled blood vessels that carry blood back towards the heart, usually under much lower pressure than arteries. With the important exception of the pulmonary vein, which carries oxygenated blood from the lungs, most veins carry deoxygenated blood back from the body's tissues. Many veins contain one way valves along their length that prevent blood from flowing backwards, which is especially important in the limbs, where blood must travel upward against gravity to return to the heart.

questions.q: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
questions.e: Arteries Arteries are thick walled, muscular blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart, usually under high pressure, since they must withstand the force of each heartbeat.

questions.q: Which blood vessels carry blood back towards the heart?
questions.e: Veins Veins are thinner walled blood vessels that carry blood back towards the heart, usually under much lower pressure than arteries.

pages.title: Capillaries
pages.body: Capillaries are extremely narrow, thin walled blood vessels that connect the smallest arteries to the smallest veins, forming a vast network that reaches almost every cell in the body. Their walls are only one cell thick, which allows oxygen, nutrients, carbon (IV) oxide and other substances to pass easily between the blood and the surrounding body tissues by diffusion. Capillaries are where the actual exchange of materials between blood and body cells takes place, making them the functional endpoint of the entire circulatory journey.

pages.title: The Chambers, Vessels and Valves of the Mammalian Heart
pages.body:
| **PART** | **DESCRIPTION AND FUNCTION** |
|---|---|
| **Right atrium** | Receives deoxygenated blood from the body through the venae cavae |
| **Right ventricle** | Pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs through the pulmonary artery |
| **Left atrium** | Receives oxygenated blood from the lungs through the pulmonary veins |
| **Left ventricle** | Pumps oxygenated blood to the whole body through the aorta. Its wall is the thickest because it pumps blood the farthest |
| **Septum** | The muscular wall that separates the right side from the left side, so that deoxygenated and oxygenated blood do not mix |
| **Valves** | The tricuspid valve on the right and the bicuspid valve on the left lie between each atrium and ventricle. Semilunar valves lie at the start of the pulmonary artery and the aorta. All valves keep blood flowing in one direction |
| **Coronary arteries** | Supply the heart muscle itself with food and oxygen |

Blood passes through the heart twice in each complete journey round the body. This is called double circulation. In the pulmonary circulation blood flows from the right ventricle to the lungs and back to the left atrium. In the systemic circulation blood flows from the left ventricle to the rest of the body and back to the right atrium. The path of the blood is body, venae cavae, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary veins, left atrium, left ventricle, aorta and back to the body.

| **FEATURE** | **ARTERIES** | **VEINS** | **CAPILLARIES** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Direction of flow** | Away from the heart | Towards the heart | From arteries to veins, through the tissues |
| **Wall** | Thick, muscular and elastic | Thinner, with less muscle | One cell thick |
| **Pressure of blood** | High | Low | Very low |
| **Valves** | Absent, except at the heart | Present | Absent |
| **Blood carried** | Oxygenated, except in the pulmonary artery | Deoxygenated, except in the pulmonary veins | Exchange food, oxygen and waste with the cells |

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

The circulatory system can be thought of as having two connected loops, a pulmonary circuit that carries blood between the heart and the lungs to pick up oxygen and release carbon (IV) oxide, and a systemic circuit that carries blood between the heart and the rest of the body to deliver oxygen and collect waste. Understanding this double loop structure helps explain why the heart has two separate sides, each specialised for one of these two circuits.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Health Challenges of the Circulatory System

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Describe the prevention and causes of diseases of the circulatory system.
- Describe what blood pressure is and ways of managing it.

pages.title: Why the Circulatory System Can Develop Problems
pages.body: Like any other body system, the circulatory system can be affected by disease, poor lifestyle habits, or underlying health conditions, sometimes with serious consequences, since every organ in the body depends on a properly functioning blood supply. Understanding common circulatory diseases, their causes and how to prevent them, alongside understanding blood pressure, gives a fuller, more health conscious picture of the circulatory system studied in Lesson 1.

pages.title: Hypertension (High Blood Pressure)
pages.body: Hypertension is a condition in which the force of blood pushing against the walls of the arteries remains consistently too high, placing extra strain on the heart and blood vessels over time. It is often caused by a combination of factors, including a diet high in salt, excess body weight, insufficient physical activity, high stress levels, smoking, and a family history of the condition. Hypertension often produces no obvious symptoms in its early stages, which is why it is sometimes called a silent condition, yet if left unmanaged, it can seriously damage the heart, blood vessels, kidneys and eyes over time.

pages.title: Atherosclerosis and Heart Disease
pages.body: Atherosclerosis is the gradual build up of fatty deposits, called plaques, along the inner walls of arteries, which narrows the space available for blood to flow through. This narrowing can reduce blood supply to important organs, and if a plaque ruptures or a blood clot forms at the narrowed site, it can completely block blood flow, potentially causing a heart attack, if it happens in an artery supplying the heart, or a stroke, if it happens in an artery supplying the brain. Atherosclerosis is strongly linked to diets high in unhealthy fats, lack of exercise, smoking and long term, poorly managed hypertension.

pages.title: Anaemia
pages.body:
Anaemia is a condition in which the blood contains fewer red blood cells, or less haemoglobin, than normal, reducing the blood's ability to carry oxygen efficiently. Common causes include a diet lacking sufficient iron, certain infections, and some inherited blood disorders. A person with anaemia often feels tired, weak and short of breath, since their tissues are not receiving oxygen as efficiently as they should.

[[pic:A comparison diagram showing a cross section of a healthy, open artery beside a cross section of an artery narrowed by atherosclerosis, with fatty plaque clearly labelled along the inner wall, and a small caption showing how blood flow is restricted in the narrowed artery.]]

Notice how the space available for blood to flow through becomes progressively smaller as plaque builds up along the artery wall, which is why atherosclerosis develops gradually, often over many years, before any serious blockage occurs.

pages.title: Preventing Circulatory Diseases
pages.body: Eating a balanced diet low in excess salt and unhealthy fat, exercising regularly, avoiding smoking, managing stress, and attending regular health checkups are widely recommended ways of preventing hypertension, atherosclerosis and related circulatory diseases. Since many circulatory diseases develop gradually and quietly, regular checkups that measure blood pressure and other health indicators allow problems to be caught and managed early, often long before serious symptoms appear.

pages.title: What is Blood Pressure?
pages.body: Blood pressure is a measure of the force blood exerts against the walls of the arteries as the heart pumps it around the body, usually recorded as two numbers, a higher systolic pressure, measured while the heart is contracting, and a lower diastolic pressure, measured while the heart is relaxed between beats. Blood pressure is typically measured using an instrument called a sphygmomanometer, either the traditional type with a mercury or dial gauge, or a modern digital device, and is expressed in units called millimetres of mercury.

pages.title: Managing Blood Pressure
pages.body: Reducing salt intake, maintaining a healthy body weight, exercising regularly, limiting alcohol consumption, managing stress, and, where necessary, taking prescribed medication are common ways of managing blood pressure and keeping it within a healthy range. For individuals already diagnosed with hypertension, consistently following medical advice and monitoring blood pressure regularly at home or at a clinic helps prevent the serious complications, such as heart attack, stroke and kidney damage, that can result from long term, poorly controlled high blood pressure.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Community health programmes in Ghana increasingly promote blood pressure screening as a routine part of health checkups, recognising that hypertension is common and often undiagnosed until it causes serious complications. Learners can play a positive role by encouraging family members to attend regular health checkups and by adopting healthy habits, such as balanced eating and regular physical activity, early in life, since patterns established in youth often carry into adulthood.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Respiration and Its Relationship with Circulation

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Explain the concept of respiration.
- Explain how deoxygenated blood from circulation is oxygenated through inhalation for respiration to take place.

pages.title: What is Respiration?
pages.body: Respiration is a chemical reaction that takes place inside living cells, in which glucose reacts with oxygen to release energy, producing carbon (IV) oxide and water as by products. This is sometimes written as a word equation, glucose plus oxygen produces carbon (IV) oxide, water and energy. Respiration should not be confused with breathing, which is simply the physical, mechanical process of moving air into and out of the lungs. Breathing supplies the oxygen respiration needs and removes the carbon (IV) oxide respiration produces, but the actual chemical reaction of respiration happens deep within cells, not in the lungs themselves.

questions.q: The word equation for respiration produces
o: Glucose and oxygen only, with no products
questions.e: This is sometimes written as a word equation, glucose plus oxygen produces carbon (IV) oxide, water and energy.

pages.title: Why the Body Needs Respiration
pages.body: Every cell in the body constantly needs a supply of energy to carry out its functions, whether that function is muscle contraction, nerve signalling, active transport of substances, or building new cell material, and respiration is the process that reliably supplies this energy. Without a continuous supply of oxygen for respiration, cells quickly run short of usable energy, which is why interruptions to oxygen supply, even for a short time, can cause serious harm to sensitive tissues such as the brain.

pages.title: The Journey of Oxygen, from Inhalation to Respiration
pages.body:
Inhalation, gas exchange in the lungs, oxygen transport by the circulatory system, and respiration within cells are four connected stages describing how deoxygenated blood becomes oxygenated and eventually supplies the oxygen that cellular respiration requires.

- During inhalation, the chest expands and the diaphragm contracts, drawing air containing oxygen into the lungs through the airways.

- Within the lungs, this inhaled air reaches tiny air sacs called alveoli, where oxygen diffuses across extremely thin walls into surrounding blood capillaries, while carbon (IV) oxide carried by the blood diffuses in the opposite direction, out of the blood and into the alveoli, ready to be breathed out.

- The now oxygenated blood returns to the left side of the heart, which was studied in Lesson 1, and is pumped out through the arteries to every tissue in the body.

- Once oxygenated blood reaches body tissues, oxygen diffuses out of the capillaries and into individual cells, where it is finally used in the chemical reaction of respiration to release energy from glucose.

[[pic:A diagram showing a single alveolus surrounded by a network of capillaries, with arrows showing oxygen diffusing from the air inside the alveolus into the blood, and carbon (IV) oxide diffusing from the blood into the alveolus in the opposite direction, clearly labelled.]]

Notice that gas exchange in the lungs relies on simple diffusion across very thin, moist surfaces, working in two directions at once, oxygen moving into the blood and carbon (IV) oxide moving out, which is only possible because the walls of both the alveoli and the surrounding capillaries are extremely thin.

lessons.title: How the Respiratory and Circulatory Systems Complement Each Other

pages.title: How the Respiratory and Circulatory Systems Complement Each Other
pages.body: The respiratory system and the circulatory system depend on each other so closely that neither could achieve its purpose alone. The respiratory system is responsible for bringing oxygen into the body and removing carbon (IV) oxide, but it has no means of transporting these gases beyond the lungs themselves. The circulatory system is responsible for transporting oxygen and carbon (IV) oxide around the body, but it has no means of exchanging these gases with the outside air. Working together, the respiratory system supplies and removes gases at the lungs, while the circulatory system carries those gases to and from every other tissue in the body, and cellular respiration, the actual energy releasing reaction, can only proceed successfully because both systems perform their complementary roles continuously and reliably.

pages.title: Aerobic and Anaerobic Respiration
pages.body:
| **TYPE** | **OXYGEN** | **WORD EQUATION** | **ENERGY RELEASED** | **WHERE IT HAPPENS** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Aerobic respiration** | Used | Glucose + oxygen gives carbon (IV) oxide + water + energy | A large amount | In most living cells all the time |
| **Anaerobic respiration in muscle** | Not used | Glucose gives lactic acid + a little energy | A small amount | In muscles during hard exercise, when oxygen runs short. The lactic acid causes tiredness and cramp |
| **Anaerobic respiration in yeast** | Not used | Glucose gives ethanol + carbon (IV) oxide + a little energy | A small amount | In yeast. It is used in baking bread and in brewing pito and palm wine |

Breathing and respiration are not the same. Breathing is the movement of air into and out of the lungs. Respiration is the chemical reaction inside cells that releases energy from glucose. The two systems work together. The respiratory system brings oxygen into the alveoli and removes carbon (IV) oxide. The circulatory system carries the oxygen to the cells and brings the carbon (IV) oxide back to the lungs.

| **GAS** | **INHALED AIR** | **EXHALED AIR** |
|---|---|---|
| **Oxygen** | About 21 percent | About 16 percent |
| **Carbon (IV) oxide** | About 0.04 percent | About 4 percent |
| **Nitrogen** | About 78 percent | About 78 percent |
| **Water vapour** | Varies | More, because the air is moistened in the lungs |

The alveoli are suited to the exchange of gases. There are millions of them, which gives a very large surface area. Their walls are one cell thick and moist, and each is wrapped in blood capillaries. Oxygen passes from the air in the alveolus into the blood, where it joins with haemoglobin in the red blood cells. Carbon (IV) oxide passes from the blood into the alveolus and is breathed out.
